title: tat tvam asi
tomorrow: 'that' points far away. which word points right here?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ramanuja's tat tvam asi: both words name Brahman, and the self is the body Brahman dwells in. Today, a third school, and the last day with this saying.

Autocorrect swaps one letter, and a whole text flips its meaning. One small sound can do that. Spoken Sanskrit runs its words together: where two a-sounds meet, they melt into one long a, and the seam disappears. In the Chandogya, the refrain runs: sa atma, tat tvam asi. That is the self; that you are. Said aloud, the seam after atma can't be heard. Madhva's school hears another word hiding there. Atat. Not that.
screen: `ONE LETTER FLIPS A TEXT.` → `SOUNDS THAT MELT TOGETHER.` → `ATAT: NOT THAT?`

segments.voice: Madhva, the teacher of the Dvaita school, reads the line as sa atma, atat tvam asi. You are not that. For Madhva, the self and the Lord are really different, and the difference lasts. It isn't a flaw to get past. In his school, it's what makes devotion possible: one to love, and one who loves. His readers look again at Uddalaka's pictures, too. The bird on its string comes home to the post it's tied to. The rivers run into the sea. In each, they point out, there's something that depends and something it depends on. Now the other side, at its best. An Advaita teacher answers: the refrain keeps saying that is the self, and names the son right after; the plain flow of the sentence joins that to you. And a Dvaita reader answers back: joined isn't the same; a bird and its post are joined, and still two. Ramanuja's school stands between them, with one Brahman and the self as its body. All three schools take the Chandogya as scripture. They part ways on what its three words mean, and each has teachers who argue it with care.
screen: `ONE SEAM, TWO READINGS.` · `ATAT: NOT THAT.` · `ONE TO LOVE, ONE WHO LOVES.` · then, large: `ONE LINE, READ WITH CARE.`

segments.voice: If there's water nearby, take one slow sip. Feel it cool the mouth and go down: something your body needed and didn't make. Rest in that small dependence for a few breaths, without needing to name it.
Tat tvam asi: one Chandogya line, heard as one awareness, as one Brahman with its body, and, by Madhva, as a real difference.
Remember this: tat tvam asi, three schools, one line, read with care. Next, a new saying.

original.note: Sanskrit: atat tvam asi, 'you are not that', the Dvaita reading of the seam after sa atma.

trapdoor: what you thought: the words on the page can only be read one way.
what it means: spoken Sanskrit merges sounds, and Madhva's school hears atat, not that: the self and the Lord really different.
what a scholar hears: sa atma + atat gives sa atmatat (sandhi), the same sound as sa atma + tat; Madhva's commentary reads lasting difference and dependence.

notes: Block 'tat tvam asi', day 9 of 9 (1752–1760): the block's last day; the close points to the next block.

Madhva's split (sa atma + atat = sa atmatat) is the well-known Dvaita reading; confirm it and its source in Madhva's own commentary. Some Dvaita readers also keep 'tat tvam asi' and read it as likeness or belonging; the lesson leaves that out.
'The difference makes devotion possible' and the reading of the bird and the rivers as pictures of dependence summarize Dvaita teaching; confirm the framing with a Dvaita Keeper.

Debate: the Advaita reply (the sentence's plain flow joins 'that' to 'you') and the Dvaita reply ('joined isn't the same; a bird and its post are joined, and still two') are the lesson's compact statements of each side's case, not quotations. Confirm each side would accept its statement. The summary of three schools is meant to rank none.
The sandhi point (two a-sounds merge into one long a) is basic Sanskrit grammar; the lesson gives no count of manuscripts or editions.
